platforms.title: Is It TMJ or Just Teeth Grinding?
platforms.meta_description: Jaw pain and soreness got you wondering? How the AAOP tells a TMJ disorder apart from bruxism, by clicking sounds, timing of pain, and visible tooth wear.
platforms.body_html:
Jaw pain and soreness, and wondering if it's just from grinding your teeth? The American Academy of Orofacial Pain (AAOP) explains that a TMJ disorder and bruxism involve completely different structures. That said, long-term untreated bruxism can eventually lead to a TMJ disorder, so the two aren't entirely unrelated.

Why the same jaw pain has different causes

A TMJ disorder is a problem with the jaw joint itself, causing a clicking or popping sound when opening or closing the mouth, and in more severe cases, the jaw catching or locking so it won't open properly. The pain is often localized right at the joint in front of the ear, frequently on just one side, and gets worse with wide yawns or chewing tough food.

Bruxism comes from an entirely different tissue. It's marked by the chewing muscles becoming overworked from clenching or grinding the teeth, usually at night, producing a sore, fatigued ache. The soreness sits more in the jaw and temple muscles rather than the joint itself, and there's no clicking sound — just a tight, worked-out feeling.

How to tell them apart, and what to check

First, whether there's a clicking, popping, or catching sensation when opening or closing the mouth. The AAOP notes this is a distinctive sign that shows up almost exclusively with a TMJ disorder. Bruxism rarely produces any sound like that.

Second, whether the pain is worst first thing in the morning. Bruxism often leaves the jaw and temples at their most sore right after waking up, following a night of grinding. A TMJ disorder tends to flare with wide mouth movements regardless of the time of day.

What matters most is not leaving bruxism unaddressed for a long time. Ongoing grinding piles stress onto the jaw joint too, and can eventually lead to an actual TMJ disorder. If morning jaw pain keeps happening, getting fitted for a night guard at the dentist helps, and if the jaw clicks or won't open properly, seeing a TMJ specialist is the safe move. Worth noting: chewing gum often to "loosen up" the jaw can actually make things worse, since it keeps working the same overtired muscles.

When it's hard to tell which one is going on, it helps to check whether there's a clicking sound, whether the pain peaks in the morning, whether the teeth show flat wear, and whether anyone sleeping nearby has heard grinding sounds.

Stress and anxiety are among the biggest drivers of nighttime clenching and grinding, so working on stress levels during the day can meaningfully reduce how much grinding happens at night, alongside wearing a night guard. A TMJ disorder, on the other hand, is more often tied to a past jaw injury, arthritis in the joint, or a bite that doesn't quite line up, which is why an orthopedic or dental exam matters for pinning down the actual cause rather than just guessing from symptoms alone.

Does your jaw click when you open it, or does it just feel especially sore in the morning?
